cases.vignette: This is an adult with a kidney mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Ezra Baraban and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is an adult with a kidney mass.
cases.feedback_text: Sections show a neoplasm composed of nests within an edematous stroma. The lesional cells have ample eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and round nuclei with central nucleoli. Chromophobe carcinoma shows prominent cell borders, perinuclear haloes, and marked nuclear membrane irregularities. Low-grade oncocytic tumor shows diffuse rather than nested architecture, shows perinuclear haloes and typically labels diffusely with CK7. Ectopic adrenal cortical tissue or adenomas may occur in the kidney and could be considered but these would express SF1 and lack PAX8 expression.

cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Andrews Matoso and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
cases.vignette: This is a 47 year old male with a kidney tumor.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Andrews Matoso and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 47 year old male with a kidney tumor.
cases.histology: The lesion is a relatively well-circumscribed and consists of a mixed inflammatory infiltrate that is notable for sheets of foamy, lipid-laden macrophages. Occasional multinucleated giant cells are also present. These histologic features support the diagnosis of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, which is a distinct form of chronic pyelonephritis that occurs predominantly in pelvicalyceal areas.
cases.discussion: Neoplastic cells in clear cell renal cell carcinoma may mimic foamy macrophages; however, neoplastic cells stain positive for epithelial markers (e.g., AE1/3) and do not express macrophage markers (e.g., CD68 and CD163). Malakoplakia can present with similar histologic features as xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, but targetoid concentrically layered basophilic inclusions (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies) are characteristic of malakoplakia. Lastly, Rosai Dorfman disease is notable for macrophages with eosinophilic cytoplasm that stain positive for S100.

cases.question_text:

This is a 75 year old male with a prostate mass.
cases.source_answer: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression
cases.correct_answer: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression
cases.canonical_answer: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression
choices_raw: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression
choices: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression
cases.histology: This neoplasm consists of atrophic, poorly formed glands with multilayered and basaloid nuclei with prominent nucleoli. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplasm demonstrates diffuse nuclear expression of p63 and expresses markers of androgen axis signaling in luminal cells, including androgen receptor (AR), NKX3.1, and prostein (P501S). This neoplasm also expresses prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR). Together, these findings support the diagnosis of prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression.
cases.discussion: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression typically shows diffuse nuclear expression of p63, and the absence of basal cells can be confirmed by the lack of expression of high molecular weight cytokeratin (HMWCK). In contrast, basal cell hyperplasia and basal cell carcinoma express HMWCK but do not show PSA positivity. Likewise, urothelial carcinoma does not express PSA, as well as P501S and NKX3.1. Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression is often mixed with conventional adenocarcinoma (85% of cases).

references.text: Prostate adenocarcinomas aberrantly expressing p63 are molecularly distinct from usual-type prostatic adenocarcinomas. cases.source_answer: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
cases.correct_answer: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
cases.canonical_answer: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
choices_raw: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
choices: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
cases.histology: This neoplasm is well-circumscribed and shows predominantly papillary architecture with an arborizing proliferation of fibrovascular cores. Neoplastic cells are mostly cuboidal and have eosinophilic finely granular cytoplasm. Notably, their nuclei are located at the apical surface opposite to the basement membrane, and the overlying luminal borders are smooth in contour. The nuclei are also small with inconspicuous nucleoli. Psammoma bodies, intracellular hemosiderin, necrosis, tight clusters of foamy macrophages, and mitotic figures are absent. These findings support the diagnosis of papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity.
cases.discussion: While neoplastic cells in renal oncocytoma show abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm with uniform nuclei, renal oncocytoma typically exhibits solid nest architecture. Papillary renal cell carcinoma can exhibit papillary architecture, but the presence of nuclei that are located at the apical surface opposite to the basement membrane is characteristic of papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity. In addition, papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity stains positive for CK7 and GATA3 and negative for CA9. In contrast, papillary renal cell carcinoma does not express GATA3. MiT family translocation-associated renal carcinoma stains negative or is only focally positive for epithelial markers. Lastly, papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity is believed to be clinically indolent and is notable for KRAS missense mutations.

references.text: Papillary renal neoplasm with reverse polarity; a morphologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular study. Al-Obaidy K, Eble J, Cheng L, Williamson SR, Sakr WA, Gupta N, Idrees MT, Grignon DJ. AM J Surg Pathol 2019; 43:1099-1111. PMID: 31135486.

Recurrent KRAS mutations in papillary renal neoplasm with reverse polarity. Al-Obaidy K, Eble JN, Nassiri M, Cheng L, Eldomery MK, Williamson SR, Sakr WA, Gupta N, Hassan O, Idrees MT, Grignon DJ. Mod Pathol 2020; 33:1157-1164. PMID: 31534204.

cases.title: Week 791: Case 3
cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth D. Thompson and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
cases.vignette: This is a 75 year old female with a pancreatic mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth D. Thompson and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 75 year old female with a pancreatic mass.
cases.histology: This neoplasm shows a solid and lobular growth pattern with fibrous bands. On higher power inspection, the neoplasm has multiple components, including formation of acini and squamoid nests. These areas of apparent acinar differentiation are predominant, consisting of relatively uniform cells with round nuclei and granular cytoplasm that are polarized around small lumina. These areas label for cytokeratins (CK8 and CK18), BCL10, trypsin, chymotrypsin, and lipase. Sqaumoid nests, which is required for this diagnosis, consist of whorled groups of plump squamoid cells. The squamoid nests show nuclear beta-catenin labeling.
cases.discussion: Squamoid nests are absent in acinar cell carcinoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. While the patient in this case is an older female, pancreatoblastoma typically occurs in children (median age at diagnosis in children is 2.4 years). In contrast, acinar cell carcinoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor usually occur in adults. In addition, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors lack acinar markers, and solid pseudopapillary neoplasm is negative for pancreatic enzymes, including trypsin and chymotrypsin.

cases.title: Week 791: Case 2
cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth D. Thompson and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
cases.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a skin lesion.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth D. Thompson and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 60 year old female with a skin lesion.
choices_raw: Metastatic ductal carcinoma of the breast
choices: Metastatic ductal carcinoma of the breast
cases.histology: This is an oncocytic neoplasm with a solid nested architecture that involves the subcutaneous tissue. On higher power inspection, neoplastic cells are large in size and polygonal in shape. They also show vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, accompanied by abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and fibrous stroma. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplasm is positive for markers of hepatocyte differentiation, including HepPar1.
cases.discussion: Apocrine carcinoma is a dermal/subcutaneous tumor that may show tubular/glandular, papillary, and solid patterns. Metastatic ductal carcinoma of the breast and apocrine carcinoma may have significant overlaps in the morphology and immunohistochemistry staining pattern. Both may be composed of ductal/glandular structures and stain positive for CK7, ER, PR, GATA3, and androgen receptor. These tumors, however, do not express markers of hepatocyte differentiation. Lastly, melanoma is excluded by the absence of staining for markers of neural crest (S100 and SOX10) and melanocytic (HMB45, MART1, MITF) differentiation.

cases.vignette: This is a 70 year old male with a pancreatic mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth D. Thompson and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 70 year old male with a pancreatic mass.
cases.histology: This is an infiltrative neoplasm composed of large polygonal neoplastic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Hepatoid carcinoma is a very rare variant of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, with only a few cases reported in the literature. As such, the molecular landscape and clinical outcome of hepatoid carcinoma remain little understood. By immunohistochemistry, neoplastic cells express markers of hepatocyte differentiation, including HepPar1 and arginase-1.
cases.discussion: The morphology and immunohistochemical staining pattern of hepatoid carcinoma overlap with those of hepatocellular carcinoma. Clinical history and imaging studies are critical and necessary for distinguishing these entities. Hepatoid carcinoma does not express markers of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms, including synaptophysin and chromogranin. Acinar cell carcinoma is excluded by the absence of staining for BCL10, trypsin, and chymotrypsin.

cases.title: Week 790: Case 3
cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
cases.vignette: This is a 65 year old female with thickened gallbladder. A lesion is noted on the gallbladder serosa.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 65 year old female with thickened gallbladder. A lesion is noted on the gallbladder serosa.
cases.histology: The glandular proliferation is centered in the serosa of the gallbladder, which demonstrates fluid acute and chronic cholecystitis with ulceration and mural thickening. While the glands may appear irregular at high magnification, at low power one can appreciate that they are generally lobular and centered around larger ducts which focally have concentric fibrosis. The atypia is minimal, and mitotic features are not readily identified. These are the typical features of hyperplastic Luschka ducts, which are a recognized mimic of adenocarcinoma in the right upper quadrant fossa.
cases.discussion: Well differentiated adenocarcinomas may be extremely bland; however, one can expect to have more infiltrative growth, some greater degree of nuclear atypia, and perhaps perineural invasion. Collapsed liver can give a similar picture of proliferating bile ductules; however, in this case, the lesion is devoid of hepatocytes, and centered on the serosa of the gallbladder away from the liver. Adenomyosis is associated with herniation of biliary epithelium into the thickened gallbladder wall, and would consist of large sinuses and not proliferation of small ductules.

references.text: HyperplasticLuschka ducts; a mimic of adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder fossa. Singhi AD, Adsay NV, Swierczynski SL, TorbensonM, Anders RA, Hruban RH, Argani P. AmJ Surg Pathol 2011; 35:883-890. PMID: 21566517

Reference: HyperplasticLuschka ducts; a mimic of adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder fossa. Singhi AD, Adsay NV, Swierczynski SL, TorbensonM, Anders RA, Hruban RH, Argani P. AmJ Surg Pathol 2011; 35:883-890. PMID: 21566517

cases.histology: This is a clear cell neoplasm with a solid nested architecture and central fibrosis, which correlates with its low nucleolar grade. On higher power inspection, one can appreciate that there is a tendency for the nuclei to be polarized away from the basement membrane, consistent with subnuclear vacuolization. Importantly, the stroma consists of highly vascularized septa, with prominent endothelial cells and minimal hyalinization. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplasm demonstrates diffuse membranous labeling for carbonic anhydrase 9 (CAIX) and CD10, and is essentially negative for cytokeratin 7. These findings support the diagnosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
cases.discussion: The morphology of the neoplastic cells in this case overlaps with that of clear cell papillary cell tumor and TFE3 rearranged renal cell carcinomas, which frequently demonstrate subnuclear vacuoles when they harbor SFPQ-TFE3 or NONO-TFE3 gene fusions. TFEB-rearranged renal cell carcinomas also can closely mimic clear cell carcinomas and are in the morphologic differential diagnosis. The best clue to the diagnosis in this case is the high cellularity of the endothelium in the vascular septa, which strongly suggests a VEGF-driven neoplasm such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma which harbors VHL gene alterations. In this case, immunohistochemistry supports this interpretation, as diffuse CAIX labeling is not seen in translocation carcinomas and the CD10 immunoreactivity and absence of CK7 labeling argue against clear cell papillary renal cell tumor.

cases.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a breast mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 60 year old female with a breast mass.
cases.source_answer: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
cases.correct_answer: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
cases.canonical_answer: Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
choices_raw: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type
Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
choices: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type
Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
cases.histology: This is an infiltrative neoplasm composed of nests of neoplastic cells with an “inside-out” growth pattern. Specifically, in many of the clusters, one can appreciate that the luminal surface is on the outside of the cluster rather than the inside as it would be in atypical gland. There is prominent space between the nests and the stroma, which is more prominent than seen in simple retraction artifact. Focally, one can appreciate an intermediate grade cribriform ductal carcinoma in situ component, assuring us that this is a primary breast neoplasm rather than a metastasis.
cases.discussion: Invasive lobular carcinoma would feature cords of bland neoplastic cells which permeate the stroma and lack e-cadherin immunoreactivity. Since greater than 90% of the tumor consists of morules of tumor cells with the inside-out growth pattern and stromal retraction, this neoplasm qualifies as a pure invasive micropapillary carcinoma rather than a ductal carcinoma of no special type. Metastatic ovarian carcinoma is excluded by the presence of a ductal carcinoma in situ. If this is not present, confirmatory stains for GCDFP and GATA 3 (positive) and PAX8 (negative) would support primary breast origin.
